mainTopic: The udder (כחל): the ברייתא's wording, the source of רב's strict ruling, and stories about local customs of eating udders
overview: This amud opens by finishing an explanation of the ברייתא's wording: it said 'cooked' about the udder only to match its second clause. Next, רבי אלעזר asks whether any תנא taught רב his strict ruling on udders. In one version, רב יצחק בר אבודימי says he never taught it. רב made a protective fence after seeing that the people of טטלפוש did not even know that בשר בחלב is forbidden. In a second version, he taught about a nursing animal's udder but said only 'udder'. The גמרא then tells of רבין, who refused an udder dish at רב פפי's house, and אביי's argument that the dish was surely permitted. Finally, רמי בר תמרי from פומבדיתא eats udders in סורא, where people do not eat them. רב חסדא questions him about the local custom, the grape seeds he roasted with (יין נסך and theft), his not wearing תפילין, and his garment without ציצית. His answer about the borrowed garment continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the ברייתא said 'cooked' in the first clause
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא used the word 'cooked' (which suggests after-the-fact) in its first clause only to match its second clause, where even after the fact the food is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the second clause, the case 'that one cooked in its milk' is forbidden, and there even after the fact it is not allowed. So the תנא also used the word 'that one cooked it' in the first clause, to match.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes answering a question about the ברייתא's wording. The ברייתא said 'cooked' in the first clause only so that it would match the second clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'that one cooked it' sounds like a case that already happened (דיעבד). That could suggest the first clause is only allowed after the fact. The גמרא explains that the word was picked for matching style, because in the second clause the food is forbidden even after the fact, so 'cooked' fits there perfectly.

keyTerms.meaning: That one cooked it; describes something already done
After the fact; once it already happened
The first clause of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'cooked' in the first clause as a sign that it is only allowed after the fact. The גמרא is saying the word was chosen just to match the second clause.

phrases.english: [In the second clause:] that one cooked in its milk – is forbidden,
where even after the fact it is also not [allowed],
[so] the תנא also taught the first clause as 'that one cooked it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּאֲפִילּוּ דִּיעֲבַד נָמֵי לָא, תְּנָא נָמֵי רֵישָׁא שֶׁבִּשְּׁלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer that began before this point, about the ברייתא's choice of wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic matching: the wording of the first clause follows the wording of the second clause.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'cooked' implies the udder is only allowed after the fact.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word was used only to match the second clause, where even after the fact it is forbidden.

steps.title: Did any teacher teach רב that the udder is forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר arrives in ארץ ישראל and asks זעירי whether any תנא taught רב the strict ruling about the udder.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי אלעזר went up to ארץ ישראל, he found זעירי and asked him: Is there a תנא who taught רב the ruling about the udder?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about where רב's strict ruling on udders came from. רבי אלעזר asks whether רב had a source from an earlier teacher; this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, one version of רב's view said an udder roasted without first being torn is forbidden. רבי אלעזר wants to know whether this is based on a ברייתא that some תנא taught רב, or whether רב came up with it himself.

keyTerms.meaning: A teacher who memorized and recited ברייתות
Went up, meaning traveled from בבל to ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: When רבי אלעזר went up [to ארץ ישראל],
he found זעירי and said to him:
Is there a תנא
who taught רב [the ruling about] the udder?
phrases.notes: This is the strict ruling from before: an udder roasted without being torn open is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the source of רב's strict ruling on udders.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב's ruling forbidding the udder came from a תנא's teaching.

steps.title: רב made a protective fence on his own
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק בר אבודימי says he never taught רב that an udder is forbidden. רב made the rule himself as a protective fence.
steps.simpleTranslation: זעירי pointed him to רב יצחק בר אבודימי. רב יצחק בר אבודימי said to him: I did not teach him anything about the udder at all. Rather, רב found an open valley and put a fence around it.
steps.whatsHappening: The תנא who would have taught רב says he never taught him this ruling. רב created the rule on his own to protect people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the ruling is not from a ברייתא; it is רב's own safeguard. The picture of an 'open valley' means a place where people were not careful, and the 'fence' is an extra rule that keeps them away from the real איסור.

keyTerms.meaning: A valley; here, an unguarded open area
Made a fence; set up a protective extra rule

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רב's strict ruling on udders is a local safeguard, not a basic law from a ברייתא.

phrases.english: He showed him רב יצחק בר אבודימי.
phrases.notes: זעירי pointed רבי אלעזר to the person who had been רב's teacher of ברייתות.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנִי לֹא שָׁנִיתִי לוֹ
phrases.english: He said to him: I did not teach him
[anything about] the udder at all,
rather, רב found an open valley
and put up a fence in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנִי לֹא שָׁנִיתִי לוֹ כְּחָל כׇּל עִיקָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אלעזר's question from the previous step.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No תנא taught it; רב made the rule himself as a protective fence.

steps.title: The story in טטלפוש that led to רב's fence
steps.stepSummary: רב heard a woman in טטלפוש asking how much milk is needed to cook meat. He saw they did not know בשר בחלב is forbidden, so he forbade udders to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב happened to come to טטלפוש. He heard a woman asking her friend: How much milk do you need to cook a quarter-measure of meat? רב said: They have not learned that meat in milk is forbidden. He stayed there and forbade udders to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells the story that explains the 'fence' from the previous step. רב saw people who did not know the basic law of בשר בחלב, so he made a strict rule for them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An udder has milk in it, so cooking it is close to cooking meat with milk. For people who did not even know בשר בחלב is forbidden, רב banned udders completely so they would not slide into the real איסור.

keyTerms.meaning: Happened to come to a place
They have not learned; they don't know

steps.whatToRemember: According to this version, רב's ban on udders was a fence for a place where people did not know the laws of בשר בחלב.

phrases.english: For רב happened to come to טטלפוש,
he heard a certain woman
saying to her friend:
A quarter-measure of meat:
how much milk does it need to cook it?
He said: They have not learned
that meat in milk is forbidden.
He stayed and forbade udders to them.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean 'and forbade.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates and backs up the claim that רב 'fenced in a valley'.
steps.raayaObject: That רב's ruling on udders was a protective fence he made himself.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of the woman in טטלפוש who did not know that בשר בחלב is forbidden.

steps.title: A second version: he taught about a nursing animal's udder
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא reports the first version. רבי יוסי בר אבא reports that רב יצחק בר אבודימי did teach about the udder of a nursing animal, but said it as a plain 'udder'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא teaches the story this way. רבי יוסי בר אבא teaches it differently: רב יצחק בר אבודימי said, 'I taught him about the udder of a nursing animal, and because of the sharpness of רב חייא, I taught him just "udder" without details.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of רב יצחק בר אבודימי's answer. In this version he did teach something about udders, but only about a nursing animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רב made the rule completely on his own. In the second version, there was a real teaching about the udder of a nursing animal, which is full of milk. It was taught as a plain 'udder', so רב applied it to every udder.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches or reports a version of the story
A nursing animal that feeds its young

steps.whatToRemember: Two versions: רב כהנא says רב made the udder rule himself as a fence. רבי יוסי בר אבא says it came from a teaching about a nursing animal's udder that was said without that detail.

phrases.english: רב כהנא teaches it this way.
רבי יוסי בר אבא teaches [that he said]:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנָא, כְּחָל שֶׁל מְנִיקָה שָׁנִיתִי לוֹ,
phrases.english: I taught him the udder of a nursing animal,
and because of the sharpness of רב חייא
he taught him just 'udder', without details.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of רב יצחק בר אבודימי's reply from step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He did teach the udder ruling, but only about a nursing animal. Because it was said as a plain 'udder', רב applied it to all udders.

steps.title: Two sages are served an udder dish
steps.stepSummary: At רב פפי's house, an udder dish is served. רב יצחק בר יוסף eats it, but רבין does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבין and רב יצחק בר יוסף came to רב פפי's house. They were served a dish of udder. רב יצחק בר יוסף ate it. רבין did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story about udder. Two sages are served the same dish and act differently, which sets up a discussion of who was right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story connects to the earlier discussion about how strict to be with udder. One sage treats the dish as permitted and the other holds back. The next step will judge between them.

phrases.english: Ravin and Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
arrived at the house of Rav Pappi.
They brought before them a dish of udder.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef ate,
Ravin did not eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִין וְרַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף אִיקְּלַעוּ לְבֵי רַב פַּפֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the reports about רב's ruling on udder to a story showing how sages acted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two sages reacted differently to an udder dish: one ate and one refused.

steps.title: אביי argues the dish was surely permitted
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks why רבין refused. רב פפי's wife came from the home of רבי יצחק נפחא, a very careful man, so she would only cook what she had learned was permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Poor רבין, why didn't he eat? After all, רב פפי's wife is the daughter of רבי יצחק נפחא, and he was very careful in his actions. If she had not learned in her father's home that this is allowed, she would not have cooked it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי criticizes רבין for refusing. He proves the dish was permitted from the family of the woman who cooked it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is based on her household. A daughter raised by a careful sage learned the right way to prepare udder at home. So we can trust the dish without checking it ourselves.

keyTerms.meaning: A master of deeds; someone very careful in keeping מצוות

phrases.english: Abaye said: Bereaved Ravin,
phrases.notes: Literally 'bereaved one.' It's a sharp way of scolding him.

phrases.english: why did he not eat?
After all, the wife of Rav Pappi
was the daughter of Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יִצְחָק נַפָּחָא מָרֵיהּ דְּעוֹבָדָא הֲוָה,
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa was a master of good deeds.

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָאו דִּשְׁמִיעַ לַהּ מִבֵּי נָשָׁא
phrases.english: Had she not heard it in her father's house,
she would not have made it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רָבִין תַּכָּלָא, אַמַּאי לָא אֲכַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Judges the story in step 6 and shows רבין had no reason to refuse.
steps.raayaObject: The udder dish served at רב פפי's house was permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The cook was the daughter of the careful רבי יצחק נפחא and would only follow what she learned at home.

steps.title: Different customs and the man who ate thrown-out udders
steps.stepSummary: In סורא people did not eat udder, and in פומבדיתא they did. רמי בר תמרי from פומבדיתא came to סורא before יום כיפור, took the udders everyone threw away, and ate them.
steps.simpleTranslation: In סורא they did not eat udders. In פומבדיתא they did. רמי בר תמרי, also called רמי בר דיקולי, came from פומבדיתא to סורא on ערב יום כיפור. Everyone took out their udders and threw them away. He went, took them, and ate them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא describes two towns with opposite customs about udder. Then it tells a story that sets up the questioning that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that this is about local custom. Udder was allowed in פומבדיתא and avoided in סורא. A visitor followed his home custom in the stricter town, and that leads to the question of which custom he must keep.

phrases.english: In Sura they would not eat udders,
in Pumbedita they would eat udders.

phrases.aramaic: רָמֵי בַּר תַּמְרֵי, דְּהוּא רָמֵי בַּר דִּיקּוּלֵי,
phrases.english: Rami bar Tamrei, who is Rami bar Dikulei,
from Pumbedita, arrived in Sura
on the eve of Yom Kippur.
Everyone took out their udders and threw them away.
He went, gathered them, and ate them.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּסוּרָא לָא אָכְלִי כַּחְלֵי, בְּפוּמְבְּדִיתָא אָכְלִי כַּחְלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about udder, this time about different local customs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סורא did not eat udders and פומבדיתא did. A visitor from פומבדיתא ate udders in סורא.

steps.title: רב חסדא asks why he did this
steps.stepSummary: The people bring רמי בר תמרי to רב חסדא, who asks him why he acted this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: They brought him before רב חסדא. רב חסדא said to him: Why did you do this?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי is brought to a judge. רב חסדא challenges him for going against the local custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question looks simple, but it is really a challenge. In סורא people avoid udder, and he ate it publicly. רב חסדא wants him to justify it.

phrases.english: They brought him before Rav Ḥisda.
He said to him: Why did you do this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges what רמי בר תמרי did in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רמי בר תמרי eating udders in סורא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He went against the accepted custom of the town he was in.

steps.title: I come from a place where udder is eaten
steps.stepSummary: He answers that he comes from רב יהודה's town, פומבדיתא, where people eat udder.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am from the place of רב יהודה, who eats udder.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי defends himself by pointing to his home custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He argues that in his home town, under רב יהודה, udder is permitted. So in his eyes he did nothing wrong. The next step tests whether a home custom is enough.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מֵאַתְרָא דְּרַב יְהוּדָה אֲנָא, דְּאָכֵיל.
phrases.english: He said to him: I am from the place of Rav Yehuda, who eats udders.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Relying on the custom of his home town
steps.terutzMaskana: He followed his own town's permissive custom.

steps.title: A traveler keeps the stricter rules of both places
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא pushes back. The rule is that a traveler must keep the stringencies of the place he left and of the place he came to.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Don't you hold that we put on him the stricter rules of the place he came from and the stricter rules of the place he went to?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא rejects the defense with a known rule about travelers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A visitor cannot use his home's leniency in a stricter town. He must keep the stricter practice of both places. Since סורא is strict about udder, he should not have eaten it.
steps.whatToRemember: A traveler must keep the stringencies of both his home town and the town he is visiting.

phrases.english: He said to him: And do you not hold that

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתְנִין עָלָיו חוּמְרֵי הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁיָּצָא מִשָּׁם
phrases.english: we impose upon him the stringencies of the place he left
and the stringencies of the place to which he went?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵית לָךְ נוֹתְנִין עָלָיו חוּמְרֵי הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁיָּצָא מִשָּׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the home-custom defense from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that his home custom permits him
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A visitor must also keep the stricter custom of the place he visits.

steps.title: He ate them outside the town boundary
steps.stepSummary: He answers that he ate the udders outside סורא's boundary, where the town's custom did not bind him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I ate them outside the boundary.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי answers that he did not eat inside סורא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The traveler's rule applies inside the town he is visiting. Once he went outside its boundary, סורא's stricter custom no longer bound him. So he did not break the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Outside the boundary of the town

phrases.english: He said to him: I ate them outside the boundary.
phrases.notes: He means outside סורא's area, where its custom doesn't apply.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the traveler's-rule challenge.
steps.terutzMaskana: He ate outside סורא's boundary, so its custom did not apply.

steps.title: What did you roast them with?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא asks what fuel he used to roast the udders.
steps.simpleTranslation: And with what did you roast them?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא opens a new line of questioning about the fire he cooked with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if eating the udders was allowed, the fuel he cooked with might have been forbidden. This question sets up the next challenge.

phrases.english: And with what did you roast them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from where he ate to how he cooked.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What fuel was used to roast the udders

steps.title: He roasted them with grape seeds
steps.stepSummary: He answers that he used grape seeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: With grape seeds.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי says he used grape seeds as fuel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer opens a new worry. Grape seeds come from wine-making, and the wine could be connected to idol worship.

keyTerms.meaning: Grape seeds left over from making wine

phrases.english: He said to him: With grape seeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He used grape seeds as fuel.

steps.title: Maybe the seeds came from idolatrous wine
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא worries the seeds might come from יין נסך, which is forbidden for any use.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe they were from יין נסך?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא challenges the use of the grape seeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יין נסך is wine connected to idol worship, and one may not get any benefit from it. Using its seeds as fuel would count as benefit. So the cooking itself might have been forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Wine poured for idol worship; one may not get any benefit from it

phrases.english: But perhaps they were from wine of libation?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean 'they were.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The seeds might come from יין נסך, which one may not benefit from.

steps.title: The seeds were over twelve months old
steps.stepSummary: He answers that the seeds were already more than twelve months old.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: They were from after twelve months.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי answers the יין נסך challenge. The questioning about the seeds goes on in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After twelve months, grape seeds are treated as having lost any forbidden wine that was still in them. So even if they once came from יין נסך, they were permitted to use by then. This answers only the איסור הנאה worry. רב חסדא raises a different worry about the same seeds in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְאַחַר שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ הֲווֹ.
phrases.english: He said to him: They were from after twelve months.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the יין נסך challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The seeds might be forbidden as יין נסך.
steps.terutzMaskana: After twelve months the seeds are permitted for use.

steps.title: Maybe the grape seeds were stolen
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא raises a new worry: perhaps the grape seeds used as fuel belonged to someone else, so taking them would be גזל.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the seeds were stolen property?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא accepts that the seeds are no longer a problem of יין נסך, but now he challenges from a different angle: maybe they were stolen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The twelve-month answer solved the איסור הנאה problem only. Even permitted seeds would still be a problem if they belonged to someone else. So רב חסדא shifts from a question about forbidden benefit to a question about ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: Stolen property; taking what belongs to someone else

phrases.english: But perhaps it was stolen?
phrases.notes: "It" means the grape seeds he burned to roast the udders.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the יין נסך worry was answered in step 16, a new objection about the same seeds is raised.
steps.kashyaTarget: רמי בר תמרי's use of the grape seeds as fuel
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even if the seeds are not forbidden for benefit, they may still belong to someone else, so using them would be גזל.

steps.title: The owners had given up on the seeds
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר תמרי answers that the owners had despaired of the seeds, since grass was growing among them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The owners had given up on them, since weeds had grown up among them.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי answers the theft worry: the owners clearly abandoned the seeds, because grass had grown over them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When owners give up hope of getting their property back, this is called יאוש בעלים, and it weakens their claim to it. The grass growing among the seeds is the evidence: no one would leave their property lying there that long unless they had written it off. This ends the series of questions about the seeds.

keyTerms.meaning: The owners' giving up hope of getting their property back

steps.whatToRemember: Every question about the roasted udders (custom, fuel, יין נסך, theft) got an answer. רמי בר תמרי was careful at each point.

phrases.english: He said to him: There was despair of the owners,
since grass had sprouted among them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the theft objection of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual clarification: the owners had abandoned the property
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The seeds might still belong to someone, making their use גזל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owners had given up on the seeds, shown by the grass growing among them, so using them was fine.

steps.title: Why aren't you wearing תפילין?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא sees that רמי בר תמרי is not wearing תפילין and asks him why.
steps.simpleTranslation: He saw that he was not wearing תפילין. He said to him: Why are you not wearing תפילין?
steps.whatsHappening: The topic moves away from the udders. רב חסדא notices that רמי בר תמרי is not wearing תפילין and challenges him about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new observation, but it follows the same pattern: רב חסדא sees something that looks wrong and demands an explanation. The question "מאי טעמא" here is not just curious. It challenges him for seemingly neglecting a מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: Phylacteries worn on the arm and head

phrases.english: He saw that he was not wearing phylacteries,
phrases.notes: רב חסדא is the one who saw, and רמי בר תמרי is the one without תפילין.

phrases.english: He said to him: What is the reason
that you are not wearing phylacteries?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new line of questioning on a different topic after the seeds discussion ended.
steps.kashyaTarget: רמי בר תמרי's not wearing תפילין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Jew should be wearing תפילין, so his not wearing them looks like neglecting a מצוה.

steps.title: Intestinal illness exempts from תפילין
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר תמרי answers that he has an intestinal illness, and רב יהודה ruled that such a person is exempt from תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I have an intestinal illness, and רב יהודה said: Someone with an intestinal illness is exempt from תפילין.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי explains that he is sick in his stomach, and he backs this up with a ruling of רב יהודה that such a person does not have to wear תפילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny the general obligation of תפילין. He shows that his situation falls under a specific exemption. Citing רב יהודה turns his personal excuse into an accepted halachic rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone with an intestinal or bowel illness

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical halachic ruling: someone with an intestinal illness is פטור from תפילין.

phrases.english: He said to him: He is suffering from intestinal illness,
phrases.notes: "He" is a polite way of saying "I". רמי בר תמרי is talking about himself.

phrases.english: and Rav Yehuda said:
One with intestinal illness is exempt from phylacteries.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 about תפילין.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Citing an exemption ruling that applies to his situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He seemed to be neglecting the מצוה of תפילין.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was exempt because of his intestinal illness, following רב יהודה's ruling.

steps.title: Why does your garment have no ציצית?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא sees that רמי בר תמרי's garment has no ציצית threads and asks why.
steps.simpleTranslation: He saw that he had not put threads on his garment. He said to him: Why don't you have ציצית threads?
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא notices another apparent problem: רמי בר תמרי's garment has no ציצית, and he challenges him about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This repeats the pattern of the תפילין challenge: an observation, then "מאי טעמא". Again the question implies that a מצוה is being neglected, and רמי בר תמרי will have to justify it.

keyTerms.meaning: Threads, here the strings of ציצית
Fringes required on a four-cornered garment

phrases.aramaic: חַזְיֵיהּ דְּלָא הֲוָה קָא רָמֵי חוּטֵי,
phrases.english: He saw that he had not placed threads,
phrases.notes: The "threads" are ציצית strings on the corners of his garment.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא לֵית לָךְ חוּטֵי?
phrases.english: He said to him: What is the reason that you do not have threads?

steps.triggerLanguage: חַזְיֵיהּ דְּלָא הֲוָה קָא רָמֵי חוּטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new observation and challenge, following the same pattern as step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The missing ציצית on רמי בר תמרי's garment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A garment that needs ציצית should have them, so wearing it without threads looks like neglecting a מצוה.

steps.title: It is a borrowed garment
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר תמרי answers that the garment is borrowed and begins to quote רב יהודה's ruling about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is a borrowed garment, and רב יהודה said:
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר תמרי explains that the garment is not his, it is borrowed, and he starts to cite רב יהודה to support this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like his תפילין answer, he does not dispute the מצוה of ציצית. He points to a special detail, that the garment is borrowed, which he will show changes the obligation. רב יהודה's actual ruling comes in the next line.

keyTerms.meaning: A borrowed garment, not owned by the wearer

steps.confusionAlert: רב יהודה's statement is not finished here. The words of his ruling continue in the next line of the גמרא, so don't think the answer is complete yet.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is a borrowed robe,
and Rav Yehuda said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the ציצית challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual clarification plus an upcoming halachic source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He seemed to be neglecting ציצית on his own garment.
steps.terutzMaskana: The garment is borrowed, and רב יהודה's ruling (continued next) is brought to explain why that matters.
